statement: Sensor bias (systematic error or statistical bias) is the non-chance, predictable component of observational error introduced by repeatable processes inherent to the measurement system. In the standard additive statistical model, a measured value $y$ relates to the unknown true value $y_{\text{true}}$ by $y = y_{\text{true}} + b + \epsilon$ (or total measurement error $e = y - y_{\text{true}} = b + \epsilon$), where $b$ is the systematic error (bias) and $\epsilon$ is the random error.

symbols.meaning: unknown true value of the quantity

properties.property: Repeated measurements and averaging do not eliminate or reduce systematic bias.
properties.why: Systematic errors arise from causes that constantly act in the same way and alter results in a predictable direction rather than fluctuating randomly.

properties.property: Sensor bias degrades measurement accuracy rather than precision.
properties.why: It offsets the observed values consistently from the true value rather than increasing the variability or standard deviation of the repeated readings.

properties.property: Sensor bias can be constant (zero error), proportional to the measured quantity, or time-varying (drift).
properties.why: Incorrect zeroing adds a fixed offset, calibration scaling defects scale with the measured quantity, and instrument condition changes (such as warming) introduce temporal drift.

properties.property: Identified sensor bias can be eliminated or compensated by recalibration or subtraction.
properties.why: Because systematic errors are predictable and reproducible rather than random, subtracting the known or estimated bias value corrects the measurement.

assumptions.assumption: Measurement error can be decomposed additively into a systematic error (bias) and a random error.
assumptions.breaks_when: Errors cannot be distinctly separated into purely systematic and random components, such as uncertainty in the calibration of an instrument.

assumptions.assumption: The systematic error remains constant when the instrument is used in the same way and in the same case.
assumptions.breaks_when: The instrument experiences temporal drift during operation (e.g., due to warming) or the bias varies as a function of the measured quantity or environmental conditions.

failure_modes.signature: Readings of a zero quantity or known baseline consistently deviate from the true value in one direction across repeated trials.
failure_modes.cause: Imperfect calibration or incorrect zeroing of the measurement instrument.

failure_modes.signature: Repeated measurements of a constant quantity display a unidirectional trend over time rather than fluctuating about a constant mean.
failure_modes.cause: Internal or environmental changes during operation, such as the instrument warming up.

failure_modes.signature: Measurement error scales in magnitude or reverses sign as a function of the true value of the quantity being measured.
failure_modes.cause: Percentage-based calibration defects or unmodeled physical effects (e.g., wave slowing in transmission media).
